title: Outbox Pattern & CDC
subtitle: Watch one order go from a database write to the search index and cache without ever losing the event.
learn: Why writing to a database and a message broker separately can silently lose events
How a transactional outbox makes the data and the event commit together
How change data capture (CDC) reads the database log to publish events without polling
Why delivery is at-least-once and consumers must be idempotent
How the same event stream keeps caches and search indexes in sync

steps.title: The order exists, the search does not
steps.body: A customer places an order. The Orders service saves it in its database. It also needs to tell the rest of the system: the search index, the cache, the email service. Those live in other systems. How do you make sure the database row and the announcement both happen, or neither does? We assume about 1,000 orders per second in this lesson.
steps.idea: One business action must change the database and notify others, and those are two different systems.
steps.caption: An order arrives and is saved in the database.

steps.title: The dual write
steps.body: The naive fix: save to the database, then publish to the broker (the message system). These are two separate writes with no shared transaction. If the service crashes, or the broker is unreachable, between them, the order is saved but the event is gone, and search never learns of it. Swapping the order does not help: you may announce an order that then fails to save. If even 0.1 percent of publishes fail at 1,000 per second, that is 1 per second, about 3,600 lost events per hour.
steps.idea: Two separate writes cannot be made atomic just by ordering them carefully. One of them can always fail alone.
steps.caption: The row is saved but the publish fails, so the event is lost.

steps.title: Transactional outbox
steps.body: Instead of calling the broker, the service writes the event into an outbox table in the same database, inside the same transaction as the order row. A transaction means both rows commit together or neither does. So the event is durable the moment the order is. Publishing becomes a separate, retryable job that reads the outbox. A broker outage can delay events but never lose them. In the HUD, lost stays 0 and one unsent row waits.
steps.idea: Use the one thing you already trust, a single local transaction, to make the data and the event inseparable.
steps.caption: The order row and the outbox row commit in one transaction.

steps.title: Who moves rows to the broker?
steps.body: Something must read the outbox and publish it. The simple way is a polling publisher. Every few hundred milliseconds it runs a SELECT for unsent rows, publishes them and marks them sent. It works, but it adds constant query load, adds delay up to the poll interval (HUD: 500 ms until the event reaches the log), and needs care to keep per-order ordering when several pollers run. The alternative is to read the database's own change log, which is next. Here the connector box plays the polling relay.
steps.idea: Polling the outbox is correct and simple. Its costs are query load and added delay.
steps.caption: A polling relay reads unsent rows, publishes them and marks them sent.

steps.title: Change data capture from the log
steps.body: Every database already writes committed changes to a log for crash recovery and replication: the write-ahead log (WAL) in Postgres, the binlog in MySQL. A CDC (change data capture) connector such as Debezium reads that log, turns each new outbox insert into an event and publishes it. It never queries your tables, sees changes in commit order, and typically delivers in tens to a few hundred milliseconds (HUD: 300 ms to reach the log). It remembers its log position so it can resume after a restart.
steps.idea: CDC turns the database's own commit log into an event stream, with no polling and no extra queries.
steps.caption: The connector tails the log and publishes the new event.

steps.title: Keeping cache and search in sync
steps.body: A sync consumer reads OrderPlaced from the event log. It adds the order to the search index and deletes or refreshes the cached entry for that customer's order list. The database stays the source of truth. The cache and index are derived copies fed by the stream. They are eventually consistent: a search may miss the new order for a moment. The HUD shows 800 ms in total: about 300 ms to reach the log plus about 500 ms for the consumer to apply it.
steps.idea: Derived stores follow the stream, so they run slightly behind the database but cannot drift apart forever.
steps.caption: The consumer updates the index and invalidates the cache.

steps.title: The connector crashes mid-publish
steps.body: Suppose the connector publishes an event, then dies before saving its log position. On restart it resumes from the old position and publishes that event again. So delivery is at-least-once, not exactly-once. The fix lives in the consumer. Each event carries a unique id, and a repeat is treated as a no-op, for example by upserting the search document by order id. In the animation, id 7f3a arrives twice and the second copy changes nothing.
steps.idea: Expect duplicates and make consumers idempotent. Do not count on exactly-once.
steps.caption: A republished event arrives twice; the consumer ignores the repeat.

steps.title: The broker is down for 90 seconds
steps.body: Orders keep committing because the service only talks to its own database. Events pile up unsent: at 1,000 per second, about 90,000 are waiting after 90 seconds, and lag grows to match (90 s). When the broker returns, the connector resumes from its saved position and drains the backlog in order. One real risk: the database must keep its log segments for the connector while it is behind, so a long outage can fill the disk. Monitor lag and cap retention.
steps.idea: The outbox keeps writes working through a broker outage, at the cost of delayed sync and a longer-retained log.
steps.caption: Events queue up in the database, then drain after recovery.

steps.title: Atomic write, then reliable fan-out
steps.body: The dual write loses events because two systems cannot commit together. The outbox puts the event in the same transaction as the data. CDC (or a poller) then moves it to the event log at least once, and idempotent consumers update caches and search indexes. You trade a little freshness and some operational care for never losing a change.
steps.idea: Commit the event with the data, ship it from the log, and remove duplicates at the consumer.
steps.caption: Order, outbox, log, consumer: no event is lost.

quiz.q: A service does INSERT into its database, then publishes to a broker. It crashes between the two calls. What is the result?
options: The broker retries and the event is still delivered
The row exists but the event is never published
The event is published but the row is missing
quiz.why: The database commit already happened and the broker call never ran. With no shared transaction, nothing remembers that an event is owed.

quiz.q: Why does the transactional outbox solve the dual-write problem?
options: It makes the broker support transactions across systems
The event is written in the same local transaction as the data, so they commit or fail together
It guarantees the broker never goes down
It publishes the event twice to be safe
quiz.why: Both the business row and the outbox row live in one database, so a single ordinary transaction makes them atomic. Publishing later is a retryable step.

quiz.q: A CDC connector restarts and re-reads a few events it had already published. What should the consumer do?
options: Process them again, since duplicates are harmless by default
Ask the connector to delete them from the log
Treat repeats as no-ops using the event ID or an upsert
quiz.why: CDC and outbox relays give at-least-once delivery, so duplicates are normal. Idempotent handling makes repeated events safe.

quiz.q: Compared with a polling publisher, what is a real advantage of log-based CDC?
options: It gives exactly-once delivery with no consumer logic
It removes the need for an outbox table in every case
It adds no query load on the tables and sees changes in commit order
It makes the cache strongly consistent with the database
quiz.why: CDC reads the commit log, so it does not run repeated SELECTs and it follows commit order. It is still at-least-once and the downstream copies stay eventually consistent.

cheatsheet.def: Writing to two systems (database and broker) in separate steps. A failure between them leaves them inconsistent, and events can be lost.
An outbox table written in the same transaction as the business data. A separate relay publishes its rows, so events are durable once the data is.
A job that periodically selects unsent outbox rows and publishes them. Simple, but adds query load and delay up to the poll interval.
Change data capture: reading a database's commit log (WAL or binlog) to emit row changes as events, in commit order, without querying the tables.
The connector's saved place in the database log. After a restart it resumes there, which is why duplicates are possible but loss is not.
A consumer that gives the same result when it sees an event twice, using the event ID or an upsert by key. Required with at-least-once delivery.
Capturing business tables directly leaks your schema to consumers. An outbox row is a deliberate, versioned event contract you control.
Monitor connector lag and retained log size. A stalled connector makes the database keep log segments and can fill disk. Clean old outbox rows.
